report.releaseDate: c. 18–19 Nov 2026 (Mississippi Gaming Commission October 2026 monthly reports; press coverage 19–24 Nov 2026)
report.currency: USD (market reports natively in US dollars; tables in $m unless stated)
report.verdict: Mississippi remains a $2.4bn-a-year, 100% land-based, low-tax (≈12% of GGR) casino market that is flat at the top line and structurally leaking sports-betting demand to mobile-enabled neighbours: October AGGR was $198.4m (-0.2% YoY; YTD -0.7%) while retail sports handle fell for a 15th straight month to $36.2m (-7.8%). The 2026 session once again saw the House pass statewide mobile wagering (100–11) and the Senate kill it in committee; with 2027 an election year and the Lt Governor publicly opposed, the operator read-through is a stable but ex-growth retail franchise with a binary, politically gated mobile option.
summary: **Market size is flat at ~$2.43bn.** Mississippi Gaming Commission (MGC) adjusted gross gaming revenue (AGGR, gross of tax) was $2,433.6m in CY2025, -0.01% on CY2024's $2,433.8m, after a -2.0% fall in 2024; Jan–Oct 2026 AGGR is $2,015.5m, -0.7% YoY, so 2026 is tracking to a third consecutive flat-to-down year.

**October 2026 AGGR was $198.36m, -0.15% YoY** ($198.66m in Oct-25), per MGC figures reported by rg.org/CDC Gaming; the trade press headline range (-0.2% to +0.2%) reflects rounding — the MGC dollar figures show a $0.3m decline. September had been +4.5% ($195.6m).

**100% land-based: online penetration is 0%.** Mississippi has no iGaming, no statewide mobile sports betting and no online lottery; mobile sports apps work only while geofenced on casino property. This is the defining structural feature of the market.

**Product mix is slot-dominated and tables are the only growth line.** October slots (EGD) win was $162.0m (-2.8% YoY; ~82% of AGGR), table games $27.7m (+9.3%), retail sports $5.25m (+27.7%). CY2025: EGDs $2.02bn (+0.2%), tables $317.7m (down), sports $49.8m (AGA/MGC).

**Geography is a three-speed market.** Gulf Coast (Coastal region) $133.1m in Oct (+0.8%; 67% share; CY25 $1,590.5m, +0.5%); Northern/Tunica $40.7m (-0.3%; CY25 $522.1m, -1.9%); Central/Vicksburg–Natchez $24.6m (-4.6%; CY25 $321.0m, +0.7%). Growth capital and table-game demand sit on the Coast; the river markets are ex-growth.

**Sports betting is in secular decline under the retail-only model.** October handle $36.19m (-7.8% YoY; lowest October since 2018's launch season; -57% vs the Oct-21 record of $83.5m); YTD handle $233.9m (-18.9% vs $288.5m), half the $468.7m of Jan–Oct 2021. CY2025 handle was $379.1m (-16.2% vs $452.4m in 2024).

**But sportsbook margin is rising on parlay mix.** October taxable revenue $5.25m (+27.7%) on a 14.5% hold (≈10.5% a year ago); parlays were 23.3% of handle but 54.3% of revenue at a 33.8% hold (15.7% in Oct-25). Football handle fell 11.0% to $17.9m (49.4% of write) yet football revenue rose 30% to $1.36m.

**Tax regime is low and GGR-based.** State licence fee is graduated on monthly GGR — 4% on the first $50,000, 6% on $50,000–$134,000, 8% above $134,000 — plus local fees averaging 3–4% (statutory cap 4%), giving a combined ≈12%; sports wagering is taxed identically plus the 0.25% federal excise on handle. CY2025 direct gaming tax was $287.9m (-0.4%), an 11.8% effective rate.

**Tax collections are tracking flat.** Mississippi DOR FY2027 gaming-tax collections were $25.40m in July 2026 and $24.08m in August 2026 ($49.47m FYTD), split General Fund $26.6m / Special Bond Sinking Fund $6.0m ($3m per month to highway bonds) / local governments $16.9m. Implied October 2026 tax at 12% of AGGR is ~$23.8m (estimate).

**Licence base: 25 commercial casinos (AGA State of the States 2026, CY2025), down from 26 in 2024**, plus three Choctaw tribal casinos (Pearl River Resort: Silver Star, Golden Moon, Bok Homa) that fall outside MGC reporting. The MGC publishes revenue by region only, not by property, so operator shares are not disclosed.

**Operator landscape is dominated by US multi-state incumbents** — MGM (Beau Rivage), Seminole Hard Rock, Boyd (IP, Sam's Town), Caesars (Harrah's Gulf Coast, Horseshoe Tunica), Penn (Boomtown, Hollywood Gulf Coast, Hollywood/1st Jackpot Tunica, Ameristar Vicksburg), Golden Nugget, Churchill Downs, Bally's, Cherokee Nation Entertainment (Gold Strike) and regional independents (Scarlet Pearl, Island View, Palace, Treasure Bay, Silver Slipper/Full House). Ownership list from public records, not re-verified against the MGC property list this cycle.

**Mobile sports betting failed for a fourth consecutive session.** HB 4074 (Mississippi Mobile Sports Wagering Act) passed the House 100–11 on 25 Feb 2026 with a 22% tax on mobile GGR, a cut in the retail casino state rate from 8% to 6% (~$48m; Lt Gov calls it a '25% tax cut'), a $6m casino protection fund and $50m/yr to the state pension system (PERS) for ten years — then died in the Senate Gaming Committee (Chair Sen. David Blount) without a hearing; companion HB 1581 died at the 3 March committee deadline.

**Political direction: Senate leadership is the binding constraint.** Lt Gov Delbert Hosemann (7–9 Jul 2026) urged the Senate to 'continue to reject' mobile wagering, citing addiction risk, cannibalisation of 'billions' of bricks-and-mortar investment and unquantified revenue; Speaker Jason White and Ways & Means Chair Trey Lamar back it, and Gov. Reeves has said he would consider a bill. 2027 is a statewide election year and Hosemann is weighing a gubernatorial run — passage odds in the Jan–Apr 2027 session are low.

**Grey-market substitution is unaddressed.** A sweepstakes-casino ban (SB 2104, 2026) died at the same committee deadline, repeating 2025's House–Senate deadlock; neighbouring Louisiana (mobile since Jan 2022), Tennessee and Arkansas offer statewide mobile, and House proponents openly concede 'everybody who wants to place wagers on their mobile device does it already today'. The MGC publishes no enforcement statistics on offshore or sweepstakes activity.

**Payments are conventional land-based rails** — cash, TITO, markers and on-property geofenced apps; the extent of cashless/digital-wallet adoption at Mississippi properties is not disclosed in MGC monthly data [unverified]. Player winnings are subject to a 3% non-refundable state withholding (Miss. Code §27-7-901).

**Responsible gambling is light-touch by benchmark standards:** age 21, an MGC-administered voluntary self-exclusion list and the Mississippi Council on Problem & Compulsive Gambling helpline; no bespoke advertising code, deposit limits or affordability rules were identified. The University of Mississippi requested $2m (Jul 2026) for gambling-harm research — a sign the social-cost argument is being institutionalised in the mobile debate.

**Competitive position vs neighbours is eroding at the margin.** Tunica's -1.9% CY2025 and Central's -4.6% October reflect Arkansas (Southland) and Louisiana (land-based plus 21.5%-taxed mobile) competition; the Gulf Coast remains a resilient drive-in destination for Alabama/Florida panhandle demand because Alabama still has no commercial casinos.

**Read-through for an operator:** Mississippi is a mature, cash-generative retail market with one of the lowest tax rates in the US and no online channel. Entry is only via acquisition of (or partnership with) one of 25 licensees; the upside case is a casino-tethered mobile regime at 22% — on our estimates $250–350m of mobile GGR at maturity ($55–77m tax), well below the sponsor's ~$100m tax claim — but timing is politically gated to 2028+ in our base case.

segments.name: Casino gaming (slots & tables) – regional dive
segments.headline: Flat $198.4m October: Coast +0.8% on tables, Tunica flat, Central -4.6% as slot win falls across all three regions.
narrative: The MGC reported October 2026 statewide adjusted gross gaming revenue of $198,356,391 against $198,663,938 in October 2025, a $0.31m (-0.15%) decline, following September's $195.6m (+4.5%). Ten-month AGGR stands at $2,015.5m versus $2,030.0m (-0.7%), which, on the CY2025 run-rate of $2,433.6m, points to a 2026 outturn of roughly $2.40–2.43bn (estimate). The month-by-month 2026 profile has been noisy rather than directional: January +4.9% ($189.0m), February +5.8% ($200.6m), March c.-5% (derived ~$214m), April +0.2% ($196.0m), May -2.6% ($217.9m), July -0.9% ($208.7m), September +4.5%, October -0.2%. There is no evidence of either a consumer break or a growth inflection; this is a mature market oscillating around a $200m monthly plateau.

Slot win remains the earnings engine and is softening: October EGD revenue was $162.0m (-2.8% YoY), with declines in every region (Coastal -1.4% to $108.8m; Northern -4.7% to $32.1m; Central -6.4% to $21.1m). Against that, table games rose 9.3% to $27.7m, led by the Coast (+9.5%) and Tunica (+12.0% to $5.9m); Central tables slipped 1.2% to $1.7m. For CY2025 the AGA/MGC split was EGDs $2.02bn (+0.2%), tables $317.7m (down) and sports $49.8m, so October's table strength is a reversal of the 2025 trend and worth monitoring for whether it reflects destination/high-end play on the Coast rather than a one-month hold effect. Product lines as reported do not sum to AGGR (~$3.4m residual in October), which we attribute to other games and rounding in the device reports.

The Gulf Coast is the only region with a credible growth story. Coastal AGGR was $133.05m in October (+0.75%), a 67.1% share of the state, and $1,590.5m in CY2025 (+0.5%), roughly 65% of the total; it is a drive-in destination market serving Alabama, the Florida panhandle and greater New Orleans, with resort-scale properties (Beau Rivage, Hard Rock, IP, Golden Nugget, Harrah's, Scarlet Pearl, Island View) and the state's only meaningful non-gaming amenity base. Northern Mississippi (Tunica, Greenville) produced $40.67m (-0.3%) in October and $522.1m (-1.9%) in CY2025, continuing a decade-long erosion as Memphis-area demand migrates to Southland (West Memphis, Arkansas). Central (Vicksburg, Natchez) posted $24.63m (-4.6%) in October after a +0.7% CY2025, and is the region most exposed to Louisiana's land-based and 21.5%-taxed mobile offer.

For an operator the commercial implication is that organic growth is unavailable statewide; share gain comes from capex-led amenity competition on the Coast or from consolidation of sub-scale river properties. The casino count has already fallen from 26 (2024) to 25 (2025); with Tunica and Central revenue per property under pressure and the tax rate too low to be a lever, the next moves are more likely closures or ownership transfers than greenfield builds outside Harrison and Hancock counties.

segments.name: Sports wagering (retail & on-premises mobile)
segments.headline: Handle down a 15th consecutive month to $36.2m (-7.8%), but a 14.5% parlay-driven hold lifted taxable revenue 27.7% to $5.25m.
narrative: Mississippi legalised sports wagering in 2018 (first bets 1 August 2018) but confined it to licensed casino premises; mobile apps are permitted only while the patron is geolocated on property. The consequence is visible in the MGC's October 2026 Sports Wagering Report: write of $36,191,686, down 7.8% from $39.3m in October 2025 and the weakest October since launch; 2021's record October was $83.5m. Handle has now declined year-on-year in every month since August 2025 (15 months). Ten-month handle is $233.9m, -18.9% on 2025's $288.5m and -50% on 2021's $468.7m; the through-October series reads 2021 $468.7m, 2022 $383.6m, 2023 $363.0m, 2024 $338.1m, 2025 $288.5m, 2026 $233.9m. Full-year 2025 handle was $379.1m (-16.2% vs $452.4m in 2024; $474.3m in 2023).

Revenue is a different story because the product mix is shifting toward high-margin parlays. October taxable revenue (the MGC's modified-accrual 'win') was $5,251,529, +27.7% YoY, for a 14.51% hold against roughly 10.5% a year earlier; at the ≈12% combined rate that yields ~$630k of tax. Parlay handle fell 19.7% to $8.4m but parlay revenue rose 72.5% to $2.85m at a 33.8% hold (15.7% in Oct-25), so parlays were 23.3% of write and 54.3% of revenue. Football remains the anchor at $17.9m (-11.0%; 49.4% of handle) with revenue +30% to $1.36m, although Central-region books lost $45,486 on football. CY2025 revenue was $49.8m (AGA, up from $41.6m in 2024, which had itself fallen 18.8%), implying a ~13.1% annual hold; note that one secondary tracker (Sportsbook Review) shows $340.4m handle / $45.4m revenue for 2025, which we treat as incomplete against the MGC-derived $379.1m.

Regionally, the Coast took $25.18m of October write (69.6%) and $3.41m of revenue (13.5% hold); Central $7.06m (19.5%) and Northern $3.96m (10.9%) together produced $1.84m on an unusually strong 16.7% hold. The Coast's football handle fell 18.7% to $12.7m while Central ($3.2m) and Northern ($2.0m) grew — consistent with Louisiana-adjacent Gulf Coast bettors having migrated to Louisiana mobile apps since January 2022, while Tunica/Vicksburg patrons face a longer drive to a mobile-legal state. Hold volatility is a real feature of a sub-$40m retail book: December 2024 produced negative statewide revenue (-$0.87m), and single-month swings of ±5pp in hold are routine.

Commercially, retail sports is now 2.6% of October AGGR and perhaps $6m of annual tax; it is an amenity, not a profit centre, and operators carry fixed sportsbook cost against a shrinking write. The value of the vertical in Mississippi lies almost entirely in the option on a statewide mobile regime, which under every House-passed draft is casino-tethered — i.e. market access would flow through the 25 licensees. HB 4074 (2026) proposed 22% of mobile GGR; applying Louisiana/Tennessee per-capita benchmarks to Mississippi's 2.94m population we estimate $250–350m of mature mobile GGR and $55–77m of tax (estimate), versus the sponsor's ~$100m claim. The $6m 'protection fund' and the 8%→6% retail rate cut in HB 4074 show that the political price of mobile will be paid by the state treasury, not operators.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: GGR-based 4/6/8% state tiers plus ≤4% local (≈12% all-in) — among the lowest in the US; licensing is property-tethered, county-opt-in and administered by the three-member MGC.
narrative: The enabling statute is the Mississippi Gaming Control Act (1990), Miss. Code Ann. §75-76, administered by the Mississippi Gaming Commission — three gubernatorially appointed commissioners and an Executive Director with investigations, enforcement, audit and laboratory divisions — with the Department of Revenue collecting gaming taxes. Casino gaming is lawful only in counties that have opted in by referendum along the Mississippi River and the Gulf Coast; post-Katrina (2005) legislation allowed Coast casinos to move onshore within a defined distance of the shoreline, and the Coast is now wholly land-based. The MGC's forms and procedures recognise operator (gaming) licences, manufacturer and distributor licences, race book and/or sports pool licences, key-employee licences and work permits, plus a separate charitable-gaming regime. Licence duration, application and investigation fees and the annual gaming-device fee schedule are not published in the monthly statistics and were not re-verified in this cycle [unverified]; the AGA's statutory summary confirms the tax structure below.

The state gaming licence fee is levied monthly on gross gaming revenue in three brackets — 4% on the first $50,000, 6% on the next $84,000 (to $134,000) and 8% on everything above — so for any casino of scale the marginal and effective state rate is 8%. Local governments levy additional fees averaging 3–4% of GGR (statutory cap 4%, split between host city/county and the county at large). Sports wagering revenue is taxed at the same state and local rates, i.e. ≈12% of taxable revenue, and is additionally subject to the 0.25% federal excise tax on handle. On CY2025 AGGR of $2,433.6m, direct gaming taxes of $287.9m (DOR via AGA, -0.4%) equate to an 11.8% effective rate; 2024 was $289.1m (-1.8%) and 2023 $294.3m. Players bear a 3% non-refundable state income-tax withholding on winnings paid by licensed establishments (Miss. Code §27-7-901).

The state's 8% is distributed by the DOR: the first $3m per month is diverted to the Special Bond Sinking Fund servicing highway bonds authorised in 1994, with the remainder to the General Fund, while the local share is transferred to host governments. FY2027 collections to date (July $25.40m; August $24.08m; $49.47m cumulative, cash basis with a one-month lag) comprise General Fund $26.6m, bond fund $6.0m and local transfers $16.9m. Those local transfers — roughly $100m a year to Harrison, Hancock, Tunica, Warren and other counties — are the political constituency that makes the Senate protective of the bricks-and-mortar model.

Compared with benchmarks (Pennsylvania 54% on slots, New York 51% on mobile sports, Illinois graduated to 40%, Louisiana 21.5% mobile), Mississippi's ≈12% is exceptionally operator-friendly, and HB 4074 would have cut the retail state rate further to 6% in exchange for a 22% mobile rate. The rule-of-thumb for an entrant is therefore that fiscal risk is low and stable, but the market is closed: there is no new-licence pathway outside the opt-in counties, and practical entry means buying or partnering with an existing licensee, with a full MGC suitability investigation of the acquirer and its key persons.

segments.name: Operator landscape & competitive position
segments.headline: 25 commercial casinos owned largely by US multi-state groups; no property-level disclosure, Coast resorts hold ~65% of revenue, Tunica consolidating.
narrative: The MGC reports revenue only by region (Coastal, Northern, Central) and does not publish property-level win or operator market shares; the AGA counted 25 commercial casinos in 2025, down from 26 in 2024 (the specific closure was not identified in our sources). Based on public ownership records — not re-verified against the MGC property list this cycle — the Gulf Coast is anchored by MGM Resorts' Beau Rivage, Seminole Hard Rock's Hard Rock Biloxi, Boyd Gaming's IP, Golden Nugget Biloxi, Caesars' Harrah's Gulf Coast, Penn Entertainment's Boomtown Biloxi and Hollywood Gulf Coast (Bay St Louis), Full House Resorts' Silver Slipper, and locally owned Scarlet Pearl (D'Iberville), Island View (Gulfport), Palace and Treasure Bay. Northern Mississippi comprises Tunica (Caesars' Horseshoe, Cherokee Nation Entertainment's Gold Strike acquired from MGM in 2023, Boyd's Sam's Town, Penn's Hollywood and 1st Jackpot, Fitz) and Greenville (Churchill Downs' Harlow's). Central comprises Vicksburg (Penn's Ameristar, Churchill Downs' Riverwalk, Bally's Casino Vicksburg, WaterView) and Magnolia Bluffs in Natchez.

Outside the commercial system, the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians operates Pearl River Resort (Silver Star, Golden Moon) and Bok Homa under IGRA; its revenue is not reported by the MGC and is excluded from all figures here. The Mississippi Lottery Corporation (sales since November 2019) is a separate state entity whose draw and scratch sales are not part of casino AGGR; its FY2026 figures were not retrieved in this cycle [n/a].

Competitively, the state's position is bifurcated. The Coast benefits from Alabama's lack of commercial casinos and from the Florida panhandle, and its $1.59bn CY2025 (+0.5%) and October +0.8% show demand is intact; investment continues to concentrate there, and table-game growth of 9.5% suggests the resort tier is winning higher-value play. The river markets face Arkansas (Southland Casino Hotel in West Memphis, with statewide mobile since 2022) in the north and Louisiana (land-based casinos in Shreveport/Baton Rouge, mobile since January 2022, tax raised to 21.5% in 2025) in the centre; Tunica revenue fell 1.9% in 2025 and Central slots dropped 6.4% in October. The number of Tunica properties has roughly halved since the 2000s and further consolidation is plausible.

For a new entrant the practical routes are: (i) acquisition of a Coast or river property (sub-scale river assets trade at low multiples but carry declining revenue); (ii) B2B supply — the on-premises sports apps and sportsbook operations at most properties are run by national brands (BetMGM at Beau Rivage, Hard Rock Bet, Caesars Sportsbook, FanDuel/DraftKings retail partnerships) [not re-verified], so platform/trading supply to independents is a niche; or (iii) positioning for a mobile licence tethered to a casino partner if and when statewide wagering passes. Given that the House drafts cap skins per casino and require revenue-sharing with the host, early partnership agreements with independents (Scarlet Pearl, Island View, Palace, Treasure Bay, Harlow's, WaterView, Magnolia Bluffs) are where optionality is cheapest.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling & enforcement
segments.headline: Conventional land-based rails, age 21, MGC self-exclusion and a helpline — no ad code, no affordability rules, and no enforcement data on offshore/sweepstakes leakage.
narrative: Because every lawful wager in Mississippi is placed on a casino floor, the payments stack is the standard US land-based one: cash at cage and kiosks, ticket-in/ticket-out, credit markers for rated play, and card/ATM access subject to the operators' own policies. Mobile sports accounts at on-premises apps are funded at the cage or via the app while geolocated on property. The degree to which Mississippi properties have adopted cashless/digital-wallet systems under MGC technical standards is not disclosed in the monthly reports and was not verified in this cycle [unverified]; there is no mobile-money or e-wallet ecosystem of the kind that defines African markets, and no statewide remote channel to which KYC/AML onboarding rules would attach. Winnings above federal thresholds trigger W-2G reporting, and the state takes a 3% non-refundable withholding at source.

Responsible-gambling architecture is minimal relative to the UK, Spain or even newer US states: the statutory minimum age is 21; the MGC administers a voluntary self-exclusion list applicable across licensed properties; and the Mississippi Council on Problem & Compulsive Gambling operates the helpline and treatment referrals, part-funded by the industry. We found no bespoke gambling-advertising code, no deposit or loss limits, no affordability checks and no statutory levy. The policy debate has, however, shifted toward harm: the University of Mississippi asked lawmakers in July 2026 for $2m to fund gambling research and public education, explicitly framed around the mobile-betting question, and the Lt Governor's July statement rested on addiction risk to young adults from '24/7 push notifications'. If mobile is eventually enacted, expect it to carry a materially heavier RG package than today's retail regime.

Enforcement direction is ambiguous. The Legislature has twice failed to ban online sweepstakes casinos — in 2025 the Senate ban was entangled with the House's mobile-betting push and died in conference, and in 2026 SB 2104 died at the 3 March committee deadline — leaving Mississippi without the explicit prohibitions adopted in states such as Montana, Connecticut, New Jersey and New York. The MGC publishes no statistics on cease-and-desist actions, illegal-machine seizures or offshore enforcement, and House leaders concede that mobile demand is already being met illegally or across state lines. For a regulated operator, this means the grey market is a competitor for the foreseeable future, and that a ban, when it comes, is more likely to be packaged with (and traded against) mobile legalisation than passed on its own.

Charitable gaming (bingo) is separately regulated by the MGC under its Charitable Gaming regulations; gross revenue data exist in the MGC's charitable-gaming series but were not retrieved for this period [n/a].

segments.name: Legislative & political direction – statewide mobile wagering
segments.headline: Four House passages, zero Senate votes: HB 4074 (22% mobile tax, 8%→6% retail cut, $6m protection fund) died in Senate Gaming Committee; Lt Gov Hosemann restated opposition in July 2026 ahead of a 2027 election year.
narrative: The 2026 regular session followed the now-familiar script. Rep. Casey Eure (House Gaming Chair) filed HB 1581, which attached a mobile framework to tidelands and child-support provisions and died unreported at the 3 March committee deadline, and HB 4074, the Mississippi Mobile Sports Wagering Act, which passed the House 100–11 on 25 February — the largest House majority yet — and was double-referred to Senate Finance and Senate Gaming, where Chair Sen. David Blount declined a hearing; it lapsed before the early-April adjournment. HB 4074's terms were designed to pre-empt the Senate's cannibalisation objection: operators must partner with a licensed casino; mobile GGR taxed at 22% (up from 18.5% in earlier drafts, pitched as the 'national average'); the retail casino state rate cut from 8% to 6% (Hosemann: a '25% tax cut', ~$48m); a $6m fund to compensate casinos showing in-person revenue declines; and $50m a year for ten years earmarked to the Public Employees' Retirement System, with the sponsor projecting ~$100m of annual revenue by reference to Tennessee ($125m) and Louisiana ($102m).

The Senate's position hardened publicly on 7–9 July 2026 when Lt Gov Delbert Hosemann, who presides over the Senate and is weighing a 2027 run for governor, posted that mobile betting 'wouldn't create a single job', carries 'a social cost that is of increasing concern', threatens 'billions' invested in land-based casinos, raises athlete-integrity risks and offers unquantified revenue, urging senators to 'continue to reject this harmful legislation'. Speaker Jason White and Ways & Means Chair Trey Lamar responded that the Senate's stance is 'tone deaf' to a market in which 'everybody who wants to place wagers on their mobile device does it already today', and that 'most every casino operator in Mississippi supports' mobile. Gov. Tate Reeves has said he would consider a bill if one reached him. Prior history: a 2023 task force (HB 606, House 109–5); HB 774 passed the House in 2024 and died in the Senate; the 2025 House bill likewise died without a Senate hearing after the House tried to fold it into the Senate's sweepstakes ban.

Our reading is that the obstacle is institutional rather than arithmetical: the Senate Gaming Committee has never been required to record a vote, local-government recipients of ~$100m of annual local gaming fees are organised against change, and the retail-tax cut needed to buy casino support simultaneously gives opponents the 'tax cut for casinos' line. With all 174 legislative seats and the statewide offices on the November 2027 ballot, the Jan–Apr 2027 session is the least favourable window in the cycle; we assign roughly a 20–30% probability to enactment in 2027 and see 2028 (post-election, new Lt Governor) as the first realistic launch-authorising session, implying go-live no earlier than 2029 (estimate).

If and when enacted, the economics are casino-tethered: skins per licensee, revenue share to the host, 22%+ tax, and likely a protection mechanism for river properties. On Louisiana/Tennessee per-capita benchmarks applied to 2.94m residents we estimate $250–350m of mature mobile GGR and $55–77m of tax, with retail sports handle likely falling a further 30–50% on launch; the sponsor's ~$100m tax figure implies ~$455m of GGR (~$155 per capita), which looks aggressive. The relevant monitoring points are bill filings in January 2027, any Senate Gaming hearing, the Lt Governor race, and whether a sweepstakes ban is used as the bargaining chip.

highlights.text: Gulf Coast is a resilient destination franchise: $1,590.5m CY2025 AGGR (+0.5%; 65% of state), October $133.1m (+0.8%) with table games +9.5% — the only region where amenity-led capex is still earning growth.

One of the lowest tax regimes in US gaming: 8% state (4/6/8% tiers) plus ≤4% local, 11.8% effective in CY2025, applied identically to sports wagering; HB 4074 would have cut the retail state rate to 6%.

Casino-tethered mobile optionality: every House-passed draft routes market access through the 25 licensees with a 22% GGR tax; early partnerships with independents (Scarlet Pearl, Island View, Palace, Treasure Bay, Harlow's, WaterView) are the cheapest way to own that option.
Sportsbook margin is improving even as volume shrinks: October hold 14.5% (vs ~10.5%), parlays 54.3% of revenue at a 33.8% hold, taxable revenue +27.7% to $5.25m and CY2025 revenue +19.7% to $49.8m.

Stable fiscal and regulatory settings: no tax changes enacted since sports betting launched in 2018, a long-standing three-member MGC, and tax collections ($49.5m Jul–Aug FY27) tracking flat — low policy-shock risk for an incumbent.
Alabama's continued absence of commercial casinos protects the Coast's eastern feeder market, and any Alabama lottery/casino legislation remains stalled.

lowlights.text: No online channel and no near-term path to one: sports handle has fallen YoY for 15 straight months (-18.9% YTD to $233.9m; -50% vs 2021) as demand migrates to Louisiana/Tennessee/Arkansas mobile apps and offshore/sweepstakes sites.

Senate leadership veto: HB 4074 passed the House 100–11 but got no committee hearing; Lt Gov Hosemann is publicly opposed and may run for governor in 2027, making the Jan–Apr 2027 session an unfavourable window (est. 20–30% passage odds).

Ex-growth core: AGGR was -2.0% in 2024, flat in 2025 and -0.7% YTD 2026; October slots fell in all three regions (-2.8% statewide), and Northern/Central markets are structurally losing share to Arkansas and Louisiana.

Grey-market crowding with no enforcement visibility: sweepstakes bans failed in 2025 and 2026; the MGC publishes no illegal-market enforcement data, and House leaders acknowledge mobile demand is already served unlawfully.

Hold volatility in a small retail book: statewide sports revenue was negative in December 2024 (-$0.87m) and Central books lost on football in October 2026; a $36m monthly write cannot absorb sharp results.
Shrinking licence base and property-level opacity: 26→25 casinos in 2025, with the MGC reporting by region only, so market-share and asset-level diligence depend on operator disclosures.

Any mobile regime will be politically priced: a $6m casino protection fund, retail tax cut and PERS earmarks mean the state, not operators, captures most of the headline value, and launch is unlikely before 2029 (estimate).

forecast.intro: There is no issuer guidance for a market, so the bridge runs from the CY2025 base to our 2026 estimate and the regulatory swing factors. CY2025 AGGR was $2,433.6m (flat); ten-month 2026 AGGR of $2,015.5m is -0.7%, with the Coast marginally positive and the river regions negative. November 2025 ($205.0m, derived) and December 2025 ($198.6m) are moderate comps, so we expect CY2026 AGGR of $2.40–2.43bn (-1% to flat; estimate) and direct gaming tax of ~$283–287m (estimate). Sports handle should finish 2026 near $310–320m (-16% to -18%; estimate) with revenue of $45–50m on a 14–15% hold. The regulatory bridge is binary: no statutory change is in force or scheduled; the only live item is re-filing of the Mobile Sports Wagering Act in January 2027 against an openly hostile Senate presiding officer.
forecast.view: Our base case is **a flat-to-slightly-down retail casino market through 2027** — Coast +0–2%, Tunica -2–4%, Central -2–5% — with aggregate AGGR holding the ~$2.4bn plateau and the effective tax rate unchanged at ≈12%. **Retail sports betting continues to shrink 10–20% a year in handle** while hold settles in the 12–15% range on parlay mix, keeping revenue roughly flat at $45–50m. **We assign only 20–30% odds to mobile wagering passing in the 2027 session** given the election calendar and the Lt Governor's stated position; a 2028 enactment with 2029 launch is our central scenario, at which point we estimate $250–350m of mobile GGR, a 22%+ tax, a 30–50% further contraction in retail sports handle, and a heavier RG/advertising package than today's regime. **Leverage of the regulatory settings is toward the state treasury**: any mobile bill will carry retail tax relief, a casino protection fund and earmarks, so the incremental value to operators is market access and data rather than tax arbitrage. Swing factors: a change in Senate leadership or committee chair; a bundled sweepstakes-ban/mobile compromise; Alabama legalising casinos or a lottery (negative for the Coast); Louisiana regulatory changes; and further Tunica closures that would reset the Northern base. For B2Tech, the actionable near-term play is B2B supply and partnership optionality with independent licensees rather than capital-intensive entry.
watch: January 2027 bill filings and whether Senate Gaming (Sen. Blount) grants the first-ever hearing on a House-passed mobile bill; House Gaming Chair Eure's tax/skin structure in the 2027 draft.
2027 statewide elections (Nov 2027): Lt Governor succession and any Hosemann gubernatorial bid — the single largest determinant of 2028 mobile prospects.
MGC November 2026 reports (due mid-December): whether slot win declines persist across all three regions and whether Coast table growth holds; CY2026 close vs our $2.40–2.43bn estimate.

Sports handle trajectory into the NFL playoffs/Super Bowl — a 16th consecutive YoY decline in November would confirm the structural leakage thesis; watch hold normalisation after October's 33.8% parlay hold.
Sweepstakes-ban legislation (successor to SB 2104) and any MGC/Attorney General enforcement actions, plus the University of Mississippi's $2m gambling-research appropriation request.
Neighbouring-state moves: Alabama lottery/casino bills, Louisiana mobile tax or market changes, Arkansas Southland performance — all direct feeders of Coast, Central and Tunica demand.
Property-level events: Tunica closures or sales, Gulf Coast capex announcements and any change in the 25-casino licence count; DOR monthly gaming-tax collections versus the FY2027 estimate.
